current_activity: D-Day: lands with the 3rd Infantry Division on Sword Beach, spearheading I Corps
notes: Event date: 6 June 1944 (Wikipedia, 27th Armoured Brigade). Event definition: The brigade, an independent GHQ formation from October 1943, is attached to the 3rd Infantry Division to spearhead I Corps in its landing at Sword Beach on D-Day (Wikipedia). Event support: one source family (Wikipedia). Wikipedia, 27th Armoured Brigade (United Kingdom): "was attached to the 3rd Infantry Division to spearhead I Corps during its landing at Sword Beach on D-Day in June 1944". Location: Sword Beach (PL0344) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the beach area; the landing places of the regiments are not given. Location support: Wikipedia names Sword Beach. Commander: Brig. G. E. Prior-Palmer, commander from 25 April 1943 (Wikipedia, 27th Armoured Brigade).

current_activity: Charnwood: supports the three infantry divisions attacking Caen from the north
notes: Event date: 8 July 1944, the first day of Operation Charnwood (Ellis, vol. I, p. 310; Wikipedia: 8 and 9 July). Event definition: For Operation Charnwood I Corps attacks with three infantry divisions (3rd British on the left, 59th in the centre and 3rd Canadian on the right), supported by the brigade and the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade and by specialised armour of the 79th Armoured Division (Ellis, p. 310); Wikipedia: on 8 and 9 July the brigade supported Operation Charnwood, the capture of Caen. Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, pp. 310-312: "supported by the 27th and 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigades"; Wikipedia, 27th Armoured Brigade (United Kingdom): "On 8 and 9 July, the 27th Armoured Brigade supported Operation Charnwood, the capture of Caen". Location: the dataset place Caen sector with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: a sector point for the attack north of Caen. Location support: Ellis and Wikipedia put the attack north of Caen and name no place for the brigade. Commander: Brig. G. E. Prior-Palmer, commander from 25 April 1943 (Wikipedia, 27th Armoured Brigade).

current_activity: Goodwood: supports the 3rd Division attack on the left flank from 07:45; Sannerville taken soon after midday
notes: Event date: 18 July 1944, from 07:45 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 343; Wikipedia gives the same hour). Event definition: On the left flank of Operation Goodwood the 3rd Infantry Division of I Corps, with the 152nd Brigade of the 51st Division under command and supported by the brigade, moves forward at 7.45 a.m. behind a barrage; Sannerville and Banneville la Campagne, well hit by the bombing, are in British hands soon after midday, while Touffreville holds out until evening (Ellis, p. 343; Wikipedia, same account). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 343: "with a brigade (152nd) of the 51st Division under command and sup- ported by the 27th Armoured Brigade, moved forward at 7.45 a.m."; Wikipedia, 27th Armoured Brigade (United Kingdom): "moved forward at 07:45 hours, supported by 27th Armoured Brigade". Location: Sannerville, Calvados (PL0727) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Sannerville, one of the two villages taken; the brigade supported the whole divisional front. Location support: Ellis and Wikipedia name Sannerville and Banneville as taken soon after midday. Commander: Brig. G. E. Prior-Palmer, commander from 25 April 1943 (Wikipedia, 27th Armoured Brigade).

current_activity: broken up: its three armoured regiments go to other formations
notes: Event date: 29 July 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 522: listed to 29.7.44); Wikipedia gives 27 July for the break-up and 29 July for the departure of each regiment. Event definition: After Goodwood the brigade is broken up and its three regiments, the 13th/18th Royal Hussars, the 1st East Riding Yeomanry and the Staffordshire Yeomanry, are distributed to other formations; Ellis lists the brigade among the independent brigades to 29 July 1944 (p. 522); Wikipedia says the brigade was broken up on 27 July and lists each regiment as leaving on 29 July. Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 522: "27th Armoured Brigade (to 29.7.44)"; Wikipedia, 27th Armoured Brigade (United Kingdom): "on 27 July 1944 the 27th Armoured Brigade was broken up"; "13th/18th Royal Hussars (left 29 July 1944)". Location: the dataset place Caen sector (representative point) with a precision of 50 km. Location approximate: a representative point; the place of the brigade headquarters when it was broken up is not given. Location support: no source read places the brigade on the day; the point is the Caen sector where it last fought. Location caveat: the day differs: Ellis lists the brigade to 29 July and Wikipedia has it broken up on 27 July; the row takes 29 July, the date both sources give for the regiments leaving (Ellis by the end of the listing, Wikipedia in the regiment list), and confidence is 0.3 for a representative point. Commander: Brig. G. E. Prior-Palmer, commander from 25 April 1943 (Wikipedia, 27th Armoured Brigade). Context: Correction to the planning list: the list said the brigade was disbanded on 29 July; the sources give 27 July (Wikipedia, break-up) and 29 July (Ellis listing and Wikipedia regiment list).
